# Data & code sharing {#data-sharing}

TADA is about your code. This chapter covers everything around it: which data to
share, in what format, with what metadata and under what licence. What a
journal's data editor will check is in the next chapter,
[The SORTEE guidelines](#sortee).

::: {.tada-note}
**On this page:** [what archiving is for](#sharing-goals) · [vocabulary](#sharing-glossary) · [what data to share](#sharing-what) · [file formats](#sharing-formats) · [metadata](#sharing-metadata) · [licences](#sharing-licences) · [checklist](#sharing-checklist)
:::

## What archiving is for {#sharing-goals}

The SORTEE guidelines set out three goals ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}). They pull in slightly
different directions, and each needs different practices.

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .neutral}
[1]{.tada-letter} [Data reuse]{.tada-word}
[Prevents data loss, enables research synthesis and meta-analysis, allows
re-analysis as methods improve, and allows new questions to be asked of existing
data, which in turn **reduces the number of animals used in
experiments**.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .neutral}
[2]{.tada-letter} [Transparency]{.tada-word}
[Readers can see what was done to obtain the reported results. Open data will
not stop fabrication, but it makes fabrication much easier to detect.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .neutral}
[3]{.tada-letter} [Computational reproducibility]{.tada-word}
[Someone else can reproduce the published results from the archived data and
code.]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

Two further points from the guidelines ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}):

- **Data are typically collected with public money**, so they can be seen as a
  public good that should not be lost when a researcher changes job or a
  computer breaks. Lost data and code are a substantial source of research
  waste.
- Published results are often **not described in enough detail to be included in
  a meta-analysis**. Archiving the data lets a synthesist re-analyse them to get
  what they need, which substantially increases the evidence available for
  synthesis.

## Vocabulary {#sharing-glossary}

Key terms from the SORTEE glossary (Table 1; [Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}). People use these terms
loosely, but the distinctions matter when someone asks you for "the raw data".
The [Glossary](#glossary) defines these and other terms used in this wiki.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Metadata** | A description of, and information about, the data and code. Typically a text file called a README; variants include a codebook or a data dictionary. |
| **Raw data** | Unprocessed and unfiltered data, including any raw files such as photos, audio recordings, videos and data sheets. |
| **Data filtering** | Removing some data to create the dataset used in the analysis, for example removing individuals with a certain characteristic. The result is **filtered data**. |
| **Data processing** | Transforming data from one form to another: extraction from images or video, summarising, transforming, calculating. The result is **processed data**. |
| **Repository** | A framework providing long-term storage for many projects, such as Zenodo, Dryad or Figshare. |
| **Project** | A collection of files archived for a specific manuscript. This is similar to what GitHub calls a *repository*, which is the source of some confusion. |
| **Data editor** | An editorial position at a journal, responsible for screening and quality-controlling the data and code archived alongside manuscripts under review. |
| **Data and code quality control** | Checking the suitability of data and code for public archiving. |

::: {.tada-note}
Transcribing data from a written to a digital format, and the error-checking
that follows, does **not** count as processing. A typed-up field sheet is still
raw data.
:::

## What data to share {#sharing-what}

Ideally, share **both raw and processed data**. The SORTEE guidelines accept
three forms, with (b) and (c) as fallbacks where a full raw upload is not
possible (Guideline 1.3; [Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}):

**a)** Raw data, along with the processed data and/or the code to prepare the
data for analysis.

**b)** A **sample** of raw data alongside the processed and filtered data, when
a full raw data upload is not possible.

**c)** Processed and filtered data with a **detailed description of how to both
obtain and process or filter the raw data**.

Raw data matter because filtering and processing are prone to mistakes, and
without the raw data nobody can check those steps. Option (c) is acceptable, but
it depends entirely on your written description being complete.

## File formats {#sharing-formats}

The rule is the same for data as for code: files should be **universally
interoperable**, meaning they can be exchanged and used across different
software and operating systems.

::: {.tabset}

### Data formats {.unlisted .unnumbered}

**Prefer simple text-based formats.** `.csv`, `.tsv` and `.txt` are the most
interoperable formats.

All verdicts below are from the SORTEE guidelines ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}).

| Format | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt` | **Preferred.** Maximally interoperable. |
| `.parquet` | Interoperable, highly compressed, efficiently read, and highly accurate for large datasets. |
| `.xlsx` | Not proprietary, so interoperable, but can carry information such as formatting that is **lost on import** into statistical software. |
| `.xls` | Proprietary format. Avoid. |
| `.RData`, `.rds` | Usable with open-source software, but requires knowledge of R to extract, and may depend on the R version used to save it. Restricts reuse. |
| `.sps` and other proprietary formats | Not interoperable; do not facilitate reuse. |
| `.pdf`, `.docx` | **Never.** Prone to error when copy-pasted, and cannot be readily imported into statistical programs. |

::: {.tada-note}
SPSS `.sps` files appear here as unsuitable, yet [Transferable](#tada-languages)
gives them as an example of a file type that passes. Both are right, because
they judge different things. This table is about **data** files, where `.sps` is
a proprietary format. The Transferable test is about **code** files, where an
`.sps` syntax file can at least be opened in a text editor.
:::

Where there is no alternative, as with data collected by proprietary software,
provide the non-interoperable file **alongside interoperable extracted data**,
and describe the conversion in the metadata, **including the software version
used**.

### Code formats {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code must be in a format that text editors and IDEs such as VS Code can open:
`.R`, `.py`, `.cpp` and so on. **Code must not be provided as a `.pdf` or pasted
into a Word document**, because copying code out of these formats can introduce
errors. [Transferable](#transferable-filetype) explains why.

:::

## Metadata: what a README must contain {#sharing-metadata}

The [Documented](#documented-readme) chapter covers the code README in detail.
The SORTEE guidelines say what is needed on the **data** side
([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}), and the two overlap heavily.

**General information**

- Manuscript title and abstract
- Authors and relevant contact information
- Date and location of data collection
- A list of all relevant funders
- Licence information, for example CC-BY
- Information about data derived from other sources, such as other articles or
  online data

**Detailed file descriptions**

- What each data file contains and how it is structured
- What variables it contains
- **What units of measurement they are in**
- How they link to the data described in the manuscript, so that every column in
  a `.csv` is explained

You can put this in the main README, in separate README files for data and code,
or in a **data dictionary** for each data file, for example a `.csv` with one
column for variable names and another for their descriptions.

::: {.tada-key}
The guidelines' standard for both data and code metadata is **"adequate"**:
detailed enough that **anyone can understand the data, or the analysis code,
without reading the manuscript** ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}). A
README that only makes sense next to your methods section does not meet it.
:::

::: {.tada-note}
Under double-blind review, some sections must be **left blank until acceptance**
and filled in then.
:::

**On LLMs.** The SORTEE guidelines add that the README should say **whether
and how the authors have used large language models in code generation**
([Resnik & Hosseini 2025]{.tada-cite data-key="resnik-2025"}), though
a data editor is unlikely to be able to verify this ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}).

## Licences {#sharing-licences}

Without a licence, data **cannot be legally reused** in many circumstances,
depending on jurisdiction, and most researchers know little about licences. The
same goes for code. Data and code usually need different licences: Creative
Commons licences such as CC0 or CC BY for data, and software licences such as
MIT or the GPL for code. The SORTEE guidelines require a licence for both, but
state a preference only for code, where they suggest permissive licences
([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}).

How to choose and attach a licence, for both data and code, is covered in
[The licence](#documented-licence) in the Documented chapter.

## Checklist {#sharing-checklist}

:::: {.tada-checklist-head}
::: {.tada-dog-float}
![](assets/figures/dog-sad.png){.tada-dog-sad alt="A sad cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
![](assets/figures/dog-happy.png){.tada-dog-happy alt="A happy cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
:::

::: {.tada-dog-hint}
Try doing all of these to make the dog happy.
:::
::::

- [ ] Raw data are archived, or a documented reason and route to them is given (option a, b or c)
- [ ] Processed and filtered data are archived, or the code that produces them is
- [ ] All data are in interoperable formats (`.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt` or `.parquet` preferred)
- [ ] Any proprietary-format file is accompanied by an interoperable extract and a description of the conversion, including software version
- [ ] Nothing lives only in supplementary material
- [ ] A data licence is chosen and stated
- [ ] A code licence is chosen and stated
- [ ] The README covers manuscript, authors, contact, collection date and location, funders, licence, and derived-data sources
- [ ] Every variable in every data file is described, **with units**
- [ ] Data and code deposits are cited in the text and the reference list
- [ ] All code used to generate results is archived, covering filtering, processing, graphing and analysis
- [ ] Seeds are set before anything stochastic
- [ ] Saved outputs are provided for anything slow or proprietary, and flagged in the metadata
- [ ] LLM use in code generation is disclosed in the README
